analysis.one_liner: Cuts the Pentagon's budget by $100 billion while sparing troops' pay and military health care.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut $100 billion from the Pentagon died in the House Armed Services Committee without a vote; it had 23 sponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut $100 billion from what Congress authorizes for the Defense Department in fiscal year 2023, keeping military personnel accounts, the Defense Health Program, and civilian federal employee pay at their prior-year levels. It states Congress's view that many urgent threats are not military and that savings should be redirected to national priorities. It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and any domestic programs that might have received the redirected savings. The bill explicitly shields military service members, veterans' and troops' health programs, and civilian defense employees from the cut, so the reduction would fall on weapons programs, operations, and contracts rather than on people's paychecks or health care.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the fiscal 2023 Defense Department authorization to the fiscal 2022 appropriated amount minus $100 billion [S3].

Protects the Defense Health Program, military personnel accounts, and civil-service pay and benefits from the reduction, so the cut would come from weapons, operations, and contracts rather than service members [S3].
States the sense of Congress that many urgent national security threats are not military in nature and that Defense budget savings should be reallocated to national priorities [S3].
Directs the Secretary of Defense to draw on the Congressional Budget Office's October 2021 study of options for operating under a smaller defense budget, rather than making arbitrary cuts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and weapons manufacturers, which would face roughly $100 billion less in authorized spending for fiscal 2023, along with Pentagon programs for weapons development, procurement, and operations not covered by the protected accounts.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts the Defense authorization during a year of war in Europe and rising U.S. security commitments; a $100 billion reduction is roughly 14 percent of the defense budget and critics would argue it risks readiness and deterrence against China and Russia [S3].

The bill does not direct the $100 billion in savings anywhere specific; reallocating it to domestic priorities is only a 'sense of Congress,' so the actual benefit to ordinary people depends on later decisions Congress could make separately [S3].

Cutting authorization without companion appropriations means the cut takes effect only if Congress later writes it into the annual spending bills, which the House and Senate leadership could refuse to do.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A $100 billion cut is real money — the protected carve-outs for troops' pay and military health mean the burden falls on weapons and operations, not service members. The main weakness is that the bill redirects nothing on its own: the promise that savings go to 'national priorities' is a statement of principle, not a spending plan. Honest supporters would acknowledge the timing (a war underway in Europe) made passage unlikely, and the bill's practical value was mostly as a marker for a larger debate about defense spending levels.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on June 13, 2022, with nine original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services [S1].
That referral was the bill's last action; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or further committee action is recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
A total of 22 House Democrats cosponsored the bill alongside the sponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and weapons manufacturers are better off, because the $100 billion reduction to authorized fiscal 2023 Defense spending never advanced. House leadership and the Armed Services Committee chair avoided a fight over a defense cut ahead of an election year, and the bill's progressive sponsors gained nothing beyond a stated position.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill cutting $100 billion from the fiscal 2023 Defense authorization and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 22 of 435 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Adam Smith (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or signaled support, leaving it in committee with no path forward.

against.name: Defense industry
against.what_they_did: The defense sector is among the largest lobbying constituencies in Washington and generally opposes major cuts to defense authorization; no defense-industry position on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat in a Democratic-controlled House; no Republican support is recorded [S4].

industries.note: The bill would cut $100 billion from the fiscal 2023 Defense authorization, directly reducing the pool of money available for weapons procurement, research, and contracts. The protected accounts (troop pay, military health, civilian pay) push the cut toward weapons and operations spending, where contractors do business [S3].

industries.industry: Military service members and civilian defense employees
industries.note: The bill explicitly shields military personnel accounts, the Defense Health Program, and civil-service pay from the cut, so their funding would stay at fiscal 2022 levels [S3].
